steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both long chains (polymers) of nucleotides, but they differ in several fundamental ways.

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon; it has –H).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   Consequence: The extra 2′-OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable (prone to alkaline hydrolysis) than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), and Thymine (T).  
   • RNA: A, G, C, and Uracil (U) in place of T.  
   Thymine has a methyl group; uracil does not. That methyl group enhances DNA stability and aids in DNA-repair recognition.

3. Strandedness and overall structure  
   • DNA: Usually double-stranded, forming a right-handed double helix (B-form in cells). Complementary strands are antiparallel and held together by hydrogen bonds (A↔T, G↔C).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded, but it can fold back on itself to make complex secondary (hairpins, stem-loops) and tertiary structures (e.g., tRNA’s cloverleaf). Some RNA viruses have double-stranded RNA genomes.

4. Length and permanence  
   • DNA: Very long (millions to billions of base pairs). Serves as a stable, long-term repository of genetic information; persists for the life of the cell or organism.  
   • RNA: Typically shorter (tens to thousands of nucleotides) and transient; synthesized when needed and degraded after it fulfills its role (an exception: some noncoding RNAs are fairly stable).

5. Cellular location  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to nucleus (eukaryotes) and also present in mitochondria and chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions largely in cytoplasm (eukaryotes). Ribosomal RNA is part of ribosomes in cytoplasm/rough ER; some RNAs stay in the nucleus.

6. Functions  
   DNA:  
      – Long-term storage of hereditary information.  
      – Template for its own replication and for transcription to RNA.  
   RNA:  
      – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries DNA’s code to ribosomes.  
      – Transfer RNA (tRNA): brings amino acids during translation.  
      – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): catalytic/structural component of ribosome.  
      – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.): gene silencing, chromatin remodeling.  
      – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes): self-splicing introns, RNase P, peptidyl transferase center.  
      – Genomic material of many viruses (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2).

7. Chemical stability & repair  
   • DNA: More stable; extensive repair mechanisms (base excision, nucleotide excision, mismatch repair).  
   • RNA: Less stable; generally not repaired—errors usually lead to degradation rather than repair.

8. Post-synthesis modifications  
   • DNA: Predominantly 5-methylcytosine in eukaryotes (epigenetic regulation).  
   • RNA: Numerous base and ribose modifications (e.g., pseudouridine, methylations) that fine-tune function.

Summary  
DNA is the durable, double-stranded, thymine-containing, deoxy sugar–based molecule that stores the cell’s genetic blueprint. RNA is the more reactive, usually single-stranded, uracil-containing, ribose-based molecule that acts as the working copy, translator, regulator, and sometimes even catalyst of that genetic information.
